node.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "This would be good for space admins, but for a typical Quora user, they would end up receiving a lot of invitations they didn\u2019t care about. It would also mean that the space admins who spent the most time sending out invitations would be the most successful. We want to create an ecosystem where space admins succeed primarily by running spaces that produce content that their audience wants, so this would work against that goal. As an admin, you can invite your followers to contribute to your space, or you can invite existing followers of the space to be contributors, or you can import email addresses of people you know outside of Quora to invite them.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

node.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "In the early days of Yahoo Answers, people wrote some high quality answers, but it didn\u2019t have systems that could scale, and so the quality went down hill quickly, to the point where it wasn\u2019t very useful to anyone. There was a similar story with Answers.com and many other traditional Q&A sites. We took a lot of lessons from those in how we built Quora early on: we focused on personalization and showing people the questions that they would be better at answering than anybody else, and showing people the answers they would want to read. To answer the question directly: we never really saw Yahoo Answers as a product we were competing against, so it wasn\u2019t particularly meaningful to hear it was shutting down.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

node.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "This threat exists, but it is mitigated somewhat by the risk that customers and merchants take on when going outside the platform. If the customer has to pay ahead of receiving the service, they risk that the merchant won\u2019t have an incentive to provide good service, and they don\u2019t have the recourse of leaving a bad review or complaining to the platform. If the customer pays after the service, the merchant takes the risk that the customer won\u2019t pay at all. Depending on how big the fees are, these risks might or might not be worth taking. The threat to the platform also tends to get higher when there is an ongoing relationship between the customer and the merchant, because then the repeated interaction can be used to build trust and mitigate the risk. node.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "First, you are right that the official reasons given for removing the feature were wrong. An internal process broke down that should have caught this and we have made some changes so that this kind of communications failure won\u2019t happen again. Since that breakdown, I actually have been personally signing off on all of these communications about product changes to prevent this going forward.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "We removed suggest edits primarily because it made development on our editors extremely complicated. We needed to make sure every feature in and around each of our editors would interact properly with suggest edits, and we need to maintain editor parity across iOS, Android, mobile web, and desktop web, so any complexity in this system gets magnified. Suggest edits was also a vector for harassment and spam, and users would sometimes get confused and accidentally accept a suggestion that they didn\u2019t mean to accept.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "The problem with having a product that is too complicated is that we can\u2019t maintain the level of product quality that we want, and we can\u2019t evolve our product over time - it means a high level of bugs and other issues, and it means less of our effort can go to making the product better so that more people can share their knowledge. With all that said, I know that a lot of people liked this feature and I hope we can bring it back someday when we have more resources to invest in this area.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

Some communities limit who can become a member, which creates meaning around the numbers. For example, if you see that a message in a private group of friends gets 20 likes, that means something very different from content that gets 20 likes on a product that is open to the whole world.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Bias the rating system", "modifiers": {"bold": true}}, {"text": ". If a rating system is doing a straight average of its inputs, then it will tend to reflect the average of the community. To avoid this, products will bias the displayed rating toward the inputs of users who are more trusted. Yelp is a good example of this approach. Their business ratings don\u2019t average in the ratings from reviews that they don\u2019t trust.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Moderate", "modifiers": {"bold": true}}, {"text": ". Some products have human moderators who watch the system and intervene in cases where it goes wrong. This can let an imperfect rating system do the brunt of the work while moderators focus their time only on the edge cases where the system isn\u2019t capable of getting it right.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Personalize", "modifiers": {"bold": true}}, {"text": ". If users are seeing a perfectly personalized ranking, then it doesn\u2019t matter if the average user likes \u201cgarbage\u201d. Personalization can happen through a follow graph that users control manually, or through algorithms that adapt to the user\u2019s activity. Because of imperfections in both of these approaches, there will still be a bias toward the average, but it won\u2019t be as bad as it otherwise would have been.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Hide ratings", "modifiers": {"bold": true}}, {"text": ". node.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "Ideally, strategy and culture will \u201cfit\u201d together, complementing each other, but they can also work against each other if they don\u2019t fit. Here are some examples I\u2019ve observed:", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "As of 2010, Google had a culture that was ideological and focused on individual users, which had been well-suited to the search market. Some examples of this were the \u201cdon\u2019t be evil\u201d motto and \u201cfocus on the user and all else will follow\u201d. After getting worried about Facebook, they made a strategic decision to invest in Google Plus. However, their culture prevented them from doing the things social networks needed to do to succeed, like making pragmatic tradeoffs that were bad for one user but would benefit the rest of the users.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Amazon\u2019s culture, focused on operational discipline, was well suited to their approach to the cloud computing market: starting with early adopters and focusing on low prices. Microsoft\u2019s culture, oriented more around sales and enterprise customers, was better suited to their approach with Azure: leveraging their existing relationships and lock-in to their existing platform. Google has had a big technology advantage which in theory should have translated into more success in the cloud computing market, but it was probably held back by their culture, which valued applying technological advances directly to features for end users, and put less emphasis on meeting the needs of non-employee developers.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Apple\u2019s culture tends to be more top down, prioritizing executives making judgments based on intuition, often without a lot of data, which is compatible with a strategy to focus energy on building a small number of new products that are often a step function better than what is available in the market. In my view, a key reason this works is the fact that Apple products are typically used by a single person at a time for a relatively straightforward purpose. This makes them easy to test and evaluate in a vacuum, without scientific experimentation. At the other end of the spectrum you have companies like Facebook or Netflix, managing complex ecosystems or with highly personalized products, where intuition doesn\u2019t generally work as well by itself and there is a need for a lot more trial and error to build a good product. There is also the capacity for a lot more trial and error in these pure internet services that can be changed at any moment for little cost, unlike the hardware Apple is producing. Consumer internet companies tend to rely much more on controlled experiments and decentralized decision-making, and this is reflected both in their strategies and in their cultures.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "The pressure for a company to generally have a single culture makes it very difficult for say Apple to do well in building services or for Google to do well in cloud computing, even if those seem like the right moves from a strategy perspective.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

node.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "First, building a product you would want to use yourself is motivating. As an example, when I was younger I programmed some games for fun, partly motivated by enjoying the process of creating them, but also motivated by the reward at the end of being able to enjoy playing them. It\u2019s rare to hear about people who create software for fun that they themselves won\u2019t use.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "This motivation makes the work more enjoyable, which makes it easier to work hard and persist for long periods of time, which is a very important factor in success and personal development. Also, other people will be more motivated to build the product for the same reason, which makes it easier to build a team, and it means they will be more motivated themselves. You will probably have friends who want to use your product, and it can be motivating to build something that they like.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Second, if you use a product yourself, your intuition will point more closely toward the right strategy for the business. Market research and experiments are useful in either situation, but sometimes there is a need to commit resources and go against the iterative ROI-maximizing path that they will point toward, maybe to break into a new market, or to get multiple interlocking changes to all fit together. In a scenario like this, having strong intuition and confidence in it is very important in designing a strategy.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "If you are not a typical customer of your product, you can build up this intuition over time as you run a company, but you won\u2019t start out with it, because you haven\u2019t been exposed to customers\u2019 preferences in a deep way. This can make it a lot harder to get initial traction or funding.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}

node.content: {"sections": [{"spans": [{"text": "I always liked programming, but I especially enjoyed competitive programming when I was in high school and college. I think its fundamental difference from normal programming comes from how contest problems are broken down into small, independent challenges. This leads to:", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Lower time commitment. With normal programming, a big project might take weeks or months of work, but a programming contest problem will take hours or even less, so you can pick them up and do them whenever you want.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "unordered-list", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "The ability to focus time on problems at the right level of difficulty. Normal programming projects consist of some work that is easy and some that is hard. Only a fraction of time on the project will generally go to the kind of work that pushes your limits at just the right level.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "unordered-list", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Faster feedback. You can learn much faster when you have a faster feedback loop. In large programming projects people often don\u2019t learn lessons for years when they see how a system is difficult to maintain or has trouble scaling. With contest problems you learn immediately what you did wrong and you can reflect on how to avoid that category of problems for next time.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "unordered-list", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "All of these properties make competitive programming problems as engaging as playing a game, but they can be much deeper than a game because of the complexity and closer connection to real-world applications. The \u201ccompetition\u201d aspect is almost incidental. It is a source of motivation for some people, but you can get most of the benefits from just doing the problems outside of a contest.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "plain", "is_rtl": false}]}
